Museum Foundation Pit
Retaining Design

Full geotechnical design for a 6.5m-deep excavation at the Liangzhu Culture Archaeological Site Park Museum, Hangzhou — from scheme selection through construction drawings.

Project Overview

The Liangzhu Culture Yuzhishan Archaeological Site Park Museum is a 2–4 storey RC frame structure with a full basement, located on an alluvial plain in Hangzhou's Linping District. The project required a retaining system capable of stabilising a 6.5m excavation across a 125,200m² footprint while protecting adjacent roads and the active archaeology park to the north and east.

The site geology presented significant challenges: the upper layers include soft silty clays (flow-plastic, φ=0.5°–7.7°) with a high groundwater table at 0.7–2.5m depth, requiring both structural support and active dewatering.

Scheme Selection

Three retaining systems were evaluated against safety, cost, constructability, and environmental impact criteria: sheet pile walls, SMW (Soil Mixing Wall), and bored cast-in-place piles. Given the complex perimeter environment and large column loads, bored piles were selected for their low soil displacement and proven performance in similar Hangzhou soft ground projects.

The final scheme pairs φ800mm bored piles at 1m spacing (23.5m length, C30 concrete, HRB400 reinforcement) with a twin-head CSM watercut curtain (φ700mm, 6.5m embedment) and a single layer of internal RC struts at 2m depth (800×800mm C30 beams, stiffness K=213.3 MN/m²). Dewatering uses a well-point system inside the pit.

Calculations & Results

Internal forces and deformations were computed across three excavation stages using the equivalent stiffness method, with the pile wall modelled as an equivalent diaphragm. Surface settlement was predicted using the Tongji parabolic model. All results comply with the Zhejiang provincial standard DB33/T1096-2014.

Key Learnings

This project required navigating genuine engineering complexity — soft alluvial soil with multiple flow-plastic layers, a high water table, and an archaeologically sensitive boundary. The scheme selection process reinforced how real decisions balance structural adequacy against constructability and cost, rather than optimising for a single metric.

Working with both the national GB standards and the Zhejiang provincial DG/TJ08 series highlighted how local practice diverges from national codes, particularly in dewatering requirements and basal heave safety factors. This dual-standard fluency is directly applicable to ConTech platforms that digitise region-specific compliance workflows.
